newsitem.title: MALAYSIA: Ringgit falls sharply, but Malaysia not loser.
newsitem.headline: Ringgit falls sharply, but Malaysia not loser.

text.p: The Malaysian ringgit has lost 5.5 percent against the U.S. dollar in the past week, but the country's trade balance remains relatively unaffected, economists and dealers said.

They said the ringgit's fall against the dollar had been offset by the U.S. unit's rise against most currencies this year, including the German mark, the Japanese yen, and the Singapore dollar, which were Malaysia's major trading partners.
"The ringgit has fallen, so what's the big deal. Every currency has lost against the big dollar this year," said a regional currency dealer with a European bank in Singapore.
"Against other currencies the ringgit has not really lost that much, which means on a trade basis the losses are not very large yet," he said.

This was why the central Bank Negara Malaysia, despite a fundamentally strong economy, had allowed the ringgit to depreciate so rapidly under the recent attack by speculators on Southeast Asian currencies, he said.

"The ringgit has gone up 1.7 percent on a trade weighted basis in the first half of this year. In July, there is downward adjustment. It could be a no gain, no loss situation," said Liew Yin Sze, regional economist with J.M. Sassoon in Singapore.
At the close of trading on Friday, the ringgit was at 2.6375/6425 to a dollar against 2.5040 a week ago.
The ringgit's slide followed de facto devaluations of the Thai baht and the Philippine peso after similar speculative attacks in the last month.
In the past two weeks, the baht has lost nearly 25 percent and the peso seven to eight percent. Indonesia too, fearing speculators, widened the rupiah's trading band to 12 percent, from eight.

Since the start of the year, the mark has fallen 16 percent to 1.79 a dollar by Friday and the yen is steady at around 116 per dollar, after weakening to 127.46 in May. The Singapore dollar has lost 4.8 percent to 1.4656 per dollar.
On Friday, the ringgit closed at 2.6375 per dollar against 2.5250 on December 31, 1996.
In 1996, the United States accounted for 18.2 percent of Malaysia's exports, the European Union 13.7 percent, Japan 13.4 percent and Singapore 20.5 percent.
Imports from these countries were 15.5 percent, 14.4 percent, 24.5 percent and 19.7 percent, respectively, of the total.

Dilip Ratha, regional economist with W.I. Carr in Singapore, said the ringgit had made substantial gains against the yen since the beginning of 1996, which offset much of the current short-term turbulence.
He added that Malaysia would be a gainer against its trading partners, particularly the United States, as exports became cheaper.
"It is cheaper for foreigners to buy ringgit now which means exports are cheaper, stocks are cheaper, all investible assets are cheaper," Ratha said.

"When the current account deficit problem was so acute the year before last, (Malaysia) contained the problem by just raising interest rates by one percentage point. The ringgit had hardly moved. Now, with the fundamentals so much better, there is no reason to worry," he said.

Malaysia raised fears of an overheating economy after reporting 9.5 percent growth in 1995. The growth eased to 8.2 percent in 1996 and the current account deficit narrowed to 5.0 percent of GDP from over 8.0 percent in 1995.

"But you cannot allow the ringgit to fall too much. It jacks up import costs, particularly necessary imports like capital goods, which account for 35-40 percent of total imports," Liew of Sassoon said.

"For the moment, Bank Negara's policy of non-interference is correct. You can either defend the currency or have low interest rates and allow the economy to grow, which the government has said is paramount," said the European bank dealer.
